title: NGC 2292 and NGC 2293
caption: The colliding galaxies NGC 2292 and NGC 2293, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2292 and NGC 2293 · constellation Canis Major · about about 120 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and W. Keel (University of Alabama)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Two glowing cores sit side by side above a bluish, curving arm, giving this pair of galaxies the look of a carved Halloween pumpkin with eyes and a crooked smile. The galaxies, NGC 2292 and NGC 2293, lie about 120 million light-years from us, toward Canis Major, and are in the early stages of a collision. The whole view is nearly 109,000 light-years across, roughly the diameter of the Milky Way.

The overall orange color comes from aging red stars, and the galaxies show only a hint of spiral structure. The eyes are dense gatherings of stars around two supermassive black holes. The smile is bluish because newborn star clusters line a new dusty arm that wraps around both galaxies. It most likely formed when gas was compressed as the galaxies began to merge.
Colliding galaxies usually lose their flat discs and become elliptical galaxies. This pair may be a rare exception, and astronomers suggest the arm may be the start of a giant new spiral.

understand.summary: Brightness detail comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through the F606W filter, while color comes from ground-based Pan-STARRS images, with the g band in blue and the z band in red.
understand.eye: Hubble supplies the fine detail in black and white, and the color is borrowed from lower-resolution ground-based images, so the picture is a blend of two sources.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, ESA, and W. Keel (University of Alabama)
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The galaxies sit far behind the crowded foreground of the Milky Way, so the field is scattered with blue foreground stars. William Keel of the University of Alabama observed the pair through the Gems of the Galaxy Zoos program, which fits short Hubble observations into gaps in the schedule, and he speculates the pair could end up like Rubin's Galaxy, UGC 2885.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Finds “Greater Pumpkin” Galaxy Pair
